title: Second brother's low opinion of musicians
summary: The brother in Oklahoma thought musicians were drunkards and dope fiends, objected to his leaving school and never forgave the change of name.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Except that the one in Oklahoma, never gave -- never -- never liked the idea of me becoming a musician. You know. Oh, they were so against it.
Was that the oldest brother?
No, that was the second brother.
Oh, he didn't like it, huh?
No, he didn't.
Didn't think it was good enough for you, huh? Good enough career?
Well no. He came to Chicago, I remember, at the end of that Chataqua thing. I know my mother had told

him and he and his wife came up, they came to see my mother, and father, and he said something about, 'You're not going to keep doing this.' I said, 'No.' I said, 'I don't know, I haven't even thought about it,' I said. -- He said, 'No, don't get thinking this way at all.' He said, 'Musicians, they're all drunkards or dope fiends and things like this. You can't -- you can't go this way at all.'
In those days they said musicians were dope fiends?
That's what he thought?
Did they?
Yeah, that's what he -- that's his opinion.
Was that right?
And he had a very low opinion of musicians. And I think he always did.
You never cured --
Yeah, he never -- he never recognized -- I changed my name, you know?
And you mean you didn't stay in touch?
No, we never stayed in touch, I never stayed in touch with him after that.
Oh.
I never saw him for years.
Oh, really. But you did stay in touch with the other brother?
I went to school that Fall and I left.
Yeah.
And he was disgruntled with that, too.
Oh, that -- it's funny that it would be the second oldest and not the oldest. The oldest was all right, huh?
